blocks.text: Every person is one of more than seventy trillion genetically different children their parents could theoretically have had, which is why siblings (other than identical twins) are alike but never the same. The machinery that shuffles the deck is meiosis, and the way it is run differs strikingly between sperm and eggs.

blocks.markdown: **Two kinds of cell division.** Somatic cells divide by **mitosis**, which produces two daughter cells that are genetically identical to the parent and diploid ($2n = 46$). It serves growth, repair and replacement. Germ cells use **meiosis** to produce **haploid** gametes ($n = 23$). Meiosis is a *reduction division* and the source of genetic variation. The diploid number must be halved in the gametes so that fertilisation restores it.

rows: Two (meiosis I and II), with one round of DNA replication
blocks.caption: Mitosis compared with meiosis.

blocks.markdown: **The stages of meiosis.** Before meiosis the DNA is replicated in S phase, so each of the 46 chromosomes consists of two sister chromatids. **Meiosis I (reductional):** in **prophase I** homologous chromosomes pair up (synapsis) in zygotene and exchange segments by **crossing over** at chiasmata in pachytene; the pairs stay joined at chiasmata through diplotene. In metaphase I the **homologous pairs** (bivalents) line up at the equator, and in anaphase I the **homologues** (not the sister chromatids) are pulled to opposite poles. This yields two haploid cells (n chromosomes, each with two chromatids). **Meiosis II (equational)** resembles a mitotic division: there is no further DNA replication, and the **sister chromatids** separate. The result is four haploid cells, each with 23 single chromatids.

blocks.title: Crossing over and independent assortment
blocks.text: Crossing over (recombination) is the reciprocal exchange of DNA segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes during prophase I. Independent assortment is the random orientation of each homologous pair at metaphase I, so the maternal and paternal chromosomes of different pairs segregate independently into the gametes.

blocks.markdown: **How variation is generated.** Three mechanisms make every gamete unique. (1) *Crossing over* creates recombinant chromosomes combining maternal and paternal alleles. (2) *Independent assortment* of 23 homologous pairs gives $2^{23} = 8{,}388{,}608$ possible chromosome combinations in a gamete even without recombination. (3) *Random fertilisation* combines one gamete from each parent. Together, the number of distinct zygotes without crossing over is about $2^{23}\times 2^{23} = 2^{46} \approx 7 \times 10^{13}$, and crossing over increases it much further.

blocks.title: Counting the gametes from independent assortment
blocks.prompt: An organism has $2n = 10$ chromosomes. How many different gametes can it make by independent assortment alone, and how many genetically different offspring combinations can two unrelated parents with this chromosome number produce, ignoring crossing over?

steps.text: The haploid number is n = 5 homologous pairs. Each pair can orient in two ways, independently.
Each parent makes 32 types of gamete, so offspring combinations equal the number of gamete pairs:

blocks.answer: 32 gamete types per parent and 1024 possible offspring genotype combinations, ignoring crossing over.

blocks.markdown: **Spermatogenesis.** Beginning at puberty and continuing throughout adult life, **spermatogonia** (diploid stem cells) in the seminiferous tubules divide by mitosis, and some enter meiosis as **primary spermatocytes** (2n, 4C DNA). Meiosis I produces two **secondary spermatocytes** (n, 2C), and meiosis II produces four **spermatids** (n, 1C). Spermatids undergo **spermiogenesis**, a differentiation process (not a division) in which the nucleus condenses, an acrosome and a flagellum form and excess cytoplasm is shed, giving **spermatozoa**. The process takes roughly two to three months. Spermatogenesis is continuous, so no stage is arrested for long, and each primary spermatocyte yields **four** functional sperm.

**Oogenesis.** In the fetal ovary, **oogonia** multiply by mitosis and the primary oocytes enter meiosis I during fetal life, but arrest in **prophase I (diplotene, the dictyate stage)** surrounded by a single layer of follicular cells in **primordial follicles**. They remain arrested until puberty or later. Of the millions of oocytes present at mid-gestation, about one to two million remain at birth, and only a few hundred are ovulated over a reproductive lifetime. Each cycle, hormonal stimulation (LH surge) causes one primary oocyte to **complete meiosis I** just before ovulation, producing a **secondary oocyte** and a small **first polar body** (unequal division of cytoplasm). The secondary oocyte immediately starts meiosis II but **arrests in metaphase II**. **Meiosis II is completed only if a sperm penetrates the oocyte**, producing a mature ovum and a **second polar body**. Each primary oocyte therefore yields **one** ovum, with the cytoplasm concentrated in it, and polar bodies that degenerate.

rows: Fetal life (meiosis I begins before birth)
Prophase I until ovulation; metaphase II until fertilisation
One ovum plus two or three polar bodies
Limited pool of oocytes, a few hundred ovulated
blocks.caption: Spermatogenesis versus oogenesis.

blocks.title: Where is each cell arrested, and what is its DNA content?
blocks.prompt: State the chromosome number and chromatid content (in terms of C, where C is the DNA content of a haploid cell after meiosis) of (a) a primary oocyte at birth, (b) the secondary oocyte at ovulation, (c) the ovum after fertilisation is triggered.

steps.text: (a) The primary oocyte has replicated its DNA and is arrested in prophase I: 46 chromosomes, each with two chromatids, DNA content 4C.
(b) After meiosis I the secondary oocyte has 23 chromosomes, each with two chromatids, arrested in metaphase II: DNA content 2C.
(c) After fertilisation triggers completion of meiosis II, sister chromatids separate: the ovum (female pronucleus) has 23 single chromatids, DNA content 1C, and the second polar body is extruded.

blocks.answer: (a) 46 chromosomes, 4C, prophase I; (b) 23 chromosomes, 2C, metaphase II; (c) 23 chromosomes, 1C, after meiosis II.

items: Meiosis I separates homologues (reduction); meiosis II separates sister chromatids.
Crossing over occurs in prophase I (pachytene) and independent assortment at metaphase I.
Spermatogenesis is continuous and yields four sperm; oogenesis yields one ovum and arrests at prophase I and metaphase II.
Variation arises from crossing over, independent assortment and random fertilisation.

blocks.title: Two arrests in oogenesis
blocks.text: A primary oocyte arrests in prophase I from fetal life until just before ovulation. The secondary oocyte arrests in metaphase II and completes meiosis only if fertilised.

points: Mitosis gives two identical diploid cells; meiosis gives four genetically different haploid cells through two divisions, with homologues separating in meiosis I and sister chromatids in meiosis II.
Crossing over (prophase I), independent assortment (metaphase I) and random fertilisation generate genetic diversity.
Spermatogenesis is continuous and yields four sperm; oogenesis arrests in prophase I (fetal life to ovulation) and metaphase II (until fertilisation) and yields one ovum.

questions.stem: Which event during meiosis I results in the reduction of the chromosome number from diploid to haploid?

options.text: Separation of homologous chromosomes in anaphase I
Separation of sister chromatids in anaphase II
DNA replication in S phase
Crossing over in prophase I

questions.correctOptionText: Separation of homologous chromosomes in anaphase I

distractorRationale.a: Correct: homologues go to different daughter cells, halving the chromosome number.
distractorRationale.b: Sister chromatid separation occurs in meiosis II and does not change the chromosome number.
distractorRationale.c: DNA replication doubles the DNA content but does not change the chromosome number.
distractorRationale.d: Crossing over generates variation but does not halve the chromosome number.

questions.explanation: Each daughter cell receives one chromosome from every homologous pair at anaphase I, so the chromosome number falls from 46 to 23. Meiosis II then separates sister chromatids without further reducing chromosome number.

questions.stem: A primary oocyte in the ovary of a newborn girl is at which stage?

options.text: Arrested in prophase of meiosis I
Arrested in metaphase of meiosis II
Completing meiosis II
Dividing by mitosis

questions.correctOptionText: Arrested in prophase of meiosis I

distractorRationale.a: Correct: oocytes arrest in prophase I (diplotene) from fetal life until ovulation.
distractorRationale.b: The metaphase II arrest occurs in the secondary oocyte at ovulation.
distractorRationale.c: Meiosis II is completed only after fertilisation.
distractorRationale.d: Oogonia divide by mitosis in fetal life, but by birth the cells have entered meiosis.

questions.explanation: Primary oocytes begin meiosis I in fetal life and arrest in prophase I within primordial follicles. They resume meiosis I only just before ovulation.

questions.stem: How many functional gametes result from one primary spermatocyte and from one primary oocyte, respectively?

options.text: Four and one
One and four
Two and two
Four and four

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a spermatocyte gives four sperm; an oocyte gives one ovum and polar bodies.
distractorRationale.c: Meiosis II produces four cells from a primary spermatocyte, not two.
distractorRationale.d: Unequal cytoplasmic division in oogenesis gives only one large functional ovum.

questions.explanation: Both meiotic divisions in spermatogenesis are equal, giving four spermatids. In oogenesis the divisions are unequal, so each primary oocyte yields one ovum and two or three small polar bodies.

questions.stem: At which stage and by what mechanism does crossing over occur?

options.text: Prophase I, by exchange of segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes
Anaphase II, by exchange between sister chromatids
Metaphase I, by random orientation of the pairs
Prophase of mitosis, by exchange between homologues

questions.correctOptionText: Prophase I, by exchange of segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes

distractorRationale.a: Correct: recombination occurs between homologues at chiasmata in prophase I.
distractorRationale.b: Sister chromatids are identical, and meiosis II does not involve recombination between homologues.
distractorRationale.c: Random orientation at metaphase I is independent assortment, not crossing over.
distractorRationale.d: Homologues do not pair in mitosis.

questions.explanation: During prophase I, homologues synapse and non-sister chromatids exchange segments at chiasmata, creating recombinant chromosomes. Independent assortment is a separate mechanism acting at metaphase I.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes the secondary oocyte at ovulation?

options.text: Arrested in metaphase of meiosis II with the first polar body extruded
Arrested in prophase of meiosis I with 46 chromosomes
A mature ovum that has completed meiosis II
Diploid and about to enter mitosis

questions.correctOptionText: Arrested in metaphase of meiosis II with the first polar body extruded

distractorRationale.a: Correct: meiosis I is completed before ovulation; meiosis II arrests in metaphase.
distractorRationale.b: This describes the primary oocyte before the LH surge.
distractorRationale.c: Meiosis II is completed only after sperm penetration.
distractorRationale.d: The cell is haploid in chromosome number and not undergoing mitosis.

questions.explanation: Just before ovulation the primary oocyte completes meiosis I, giving a secondary oocyte and first polar body, and then arrests at metaphase II. It completes meiosis II only if fertilised.

questions.stem: A species has a diploid chromosome number 2n = 14. Ignoring crossing over, how many genetically different gametes can one individual produce by independent assortment? Give a number of gamete types.
questions.explanation: With 2n = 14 there are n = 7 homologous pairs, each orienting independently at metaphase I, so the number of combinations is 2^7 = 128. Crossing over would increase variation much further.

questions.stem: Two unrelated parents each have 2n = 8 chromosomes. Ignoring crossing over, how many genetically different zygotes could they produce by independent assortment and random fertilisation? Give a number of zygote types.
questions.explanation: Each parent has n = 4 pairs and so makes 2^4 = 16 gamete types. Any gamete from one parent can combine with any from the other: 16 x 16 = 256 zygote combinations.

questions.stem: True or false: In meiosis II the homologous chromosomes separate.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Homologues separate in meiosis I. In meiosis II the sister chromatids separate, much like in mitosis, without further reduction of the chromosome number.

questions.stem: Compare mitosis and meiosis in terms of the number of divisions, the number and ploidy of the daughter cells, and the genetic variation produced.
markingGuide: Mitosis: one division; two diploid daughter cells identical to the parent; for growth and repair.
Meiosis: two divisions after a single DNA replication; four haploid cells.
Meiosis I separates homologues (reduction); meiosis II separates sister chromatids.
Meiosis generates variation by crossing over in prophase I and independent assortment at metaphase I; mitosis produces no new combinations.
Meiosis occurs only in germ cells.
questions.explanation: Mitosis conserves the genome whereas meiosis halves the chromosome number and shuffles alleles to produce unique gametes.

questions.stem: Describe oogenesis from the fetal ovary to fertilisation, stating the two points at which the cell arrests and what releases each arrest. Then name one key difference from spermatogenesis.
markingGuide: Oogonia divide by mitosis in fetal life; primary oocytes begin meiosis I and arrest in prophase I (diplotene) in primordial follicles.
Arrest in prophase I is released by the LH surge before ovulation; meiosis I is completed to give secondary oocyte and first polar body.
Secondary oocyte arrests in metaphase II; released by sperm penetration (fertilisation), producing ovum and second polar body.
One ovum per primary oocyte, unequal division of cytoplasm.
Difference: spermatogenesis starts at puberty, is continuous, gives four sperm and has no long arrests.
questions.explanation: Oogenesis starts before birth and has two arrests, whereas spermatogenesis is continuous and produces four gametes per spermatocyte.
